docs.title: Developer Guide
docs.text:
Everything you need to contribute to TorchEBM. This page takes you from a fresh clone to a merged pull request; the other three pages cover the code itself:

  • Architecture: package layout and how the core abstractions compose.
  • Code Guidelines: style, API design, performance rules, testing.
  • Performance and Benchmarking: writing fast code, and measuring it.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Requirements: Python 3.9+, Git, a GitHub account.

Fork the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork and install the development dependencies; on Windows, activate the environment with .venv\Scripts\activate:

git clone https://github.com/<your-user>/torchebm.git
cd torchebm
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"

For docs work, install the docs extra and start the live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Claim the issue. Check that nobody is assigned and no open PR already links it, then comment on the issue to say you are taking it. A PR that duplicates an earlier one for the same issue is closed in favour of the first.
  2. Branch from master with a descriptive name. 
    git checkout -b feat/adaptive-step-size
  3. Code: follow the Code Guidelines. Mirror the package layout under tests/.
  4. Test and format before every commit. 
    black torchebm/ tests/
isort torchebm/ tests/
pytest tests/ -v
  5. Commit using Conventional Commits (below).
  6. Push and open a PR against master. Link any related issue.

docs.title: Commit conventions (mandatory)
docs.text:
TorchEBM uses Conventional Commits:

<type>(<optional scope>): <summary>
Type Use for feat A new user-facing feature fix A bug fix perf A change that improves performance refactor Code change that is neither a feature nor a fix test Adding or fixing tests docs Documentation only style Formatting, whitespace, no logic change build Build system, packaging ci CI configuration chore Other maintenance (deps, tooling)

Examples

feat(samplers): add adaptive step size to LangevinDynamics
fix(losses): correct gradient sign in EquilibriumMatching
perf(integrators): cache RK buffers on device once per integrate()

Breaking changes add a ! after the type and a BREAKING CHANGE: footer. Keep the summary under 72 chars, imperative mood, no trailing period.

No AI attribution anywhere: no Co-authored-by trailers for AI tools, no "generated with" footers, no mentions of assistants in commit messages, PR titles or PR descriptions. Attribution trailers land in the contributors graph; PR text lands in the changelog. Both must name people only.

docs.title: Before opening the PR
docs.text:
• No earlier open PR targets the same issue
  • Tests pass: pytest tests/ -v
  • Formatting applied: black and isort
  • Public API changes documented in the relevant docstring
  • If you touched an example: pytest -m examples tests/examples passes
  • If performance-sensitive: benchmarked per Performance and Benchmarking
  • Commit messages follow Conventional Commits
  • No AI attribution in commits, PR title or PR description

The PR description should say what changed and why, and reference any issue it closes (Closes #123).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: TorchEBM is organised around a small set of base classes (BaseModel, BaseSampler, BaseLoss, BaseIntegrator, BaseInterpolant, BaseCoupling). Everything else is composition in the training loop: a coupling and an interpolant build the regression target, a loss compares model outputs, a sampler drives the model through an integrator. The user-facing statement of this design is Design and Scope; this page is the contributor view.

docs.title: Package layout
docs.text:
The tree below is generated from the installed package at build time (comments come from docs/hooks/gen_diagrams.py; new subpackages appear automatically):

torchebm/
├── core/          # Base classes, analytic energies, schedulers, TorchEBMModule
├── samplers/      # MCMC, optimization, and flow/diffusion samplers
├── losses/        # Training objectives (CD, score matching, equilibrium/energy matching)
├── interpolants/  # Noise-to-data probability paths
├── couplings/     # Pairings between noise and data batches
├── integrators/   # Numerical integrators for SDE/ODE/Hamiltonian dynamics
├── models/        # Neural architectures used as energies or fields
├── datasets/      # Synthetic data generators
├── utils/         # Shared helpers
└── cuda/          # Custom CUDA kernels

Mirror this layout under tests/ when adding tests.

docs.title: Core abstractions
docs.text:
One contract per axis. The table is generated at build time from the root base classes exported by torchebm.core and the first line of their docstrings, so it always matches the code:

Base class Contract BaseCoupling Abstract base class for couplings. BaseIntegrator Abstract integrator that advances a sampler state according to dynamics. BaseInterpolant Abstract base class for stochastic interpolants. BaseLoss Abstract base class for loss functions used in energy-based models. BaseModel Abstract base class for energy-based models (EBMs). BaseSampler Abstract base class for samplers. BaseScheduler Abstract base class for parameter schedulers. TorchEBMModule Base nn.Module with cached, parameter-derived device/dtype access.

The current composition map and export counts, generated from the installed package at build time (see docs/hooks/gen_diagrams.py; per-family class trees render the same way on the Concepts pages):

graph LR
    field["energy / field<br/>core: 10 analytic energies · models"]
    interp["interpolants (4)"]
    coup["couplings (7)"]
    integ["integrators (12)"]
    samp["samplers (6)"]
    loss["objectives (12)"]
    data[("datasets (8)")]
    out(("samples"))
    field --> samp
    field --> loss
    interp --> loss
    interp --> samp
    coup --> loss
    integ --> samp
    samp -- negatives --> loss
    data --> loss
    samp --> out

String registries (get_integrator, get_coupling, get_interpolant) make each axis addressable by name; resolve_* helpers validate instances against the family a consumer requires. Every component exported through torchebm.*.__init__ is auto-discovered by the benchmark suite (see Performance and Benchmarking).

docs.title: How the pieces compose
docs.text: Training is the standard PyTorch loop: the model is called on inputs, a loss function compares its outputs with targets, the optimizer steps. Losses never hold the model; samplers take it as an argument of the call, sampler(model, x, n_steps=...), the torchdiffeq form. Two patterns cover the library.

docs.title: Sampler-free (score, flow, EqM, EM warm-up)
docs.text:
The loop builds the target from data with a coupling and an interpolant: couple the batch, draw \(t\), interpolate, call the model, regress.

x0, x1 = coupling(torch.randn_like(x1), x1)
x_t, u_t = path(x0, x1, t)
loss = loss_fn(model(x_t, t), u_t)

Samplers only appear at generation time.

docs.title: Sampler-based (CD family, EM joint phase)
docs.text:
Contrastive divergence draws negatives from the current model every step, from a replay buffer for persistent chains, and the loss compares the energies of data and negatives:

graph LR
    buffer[replay buffer] --> sampler
    model --> sampler
    sampler -- negatives x_neg --> model
    data[data x] --> model
    model -- "E(x), E(x_neg)" --> loss_fn
    loss_fn -- grad --> optimizer
    optimizer --> model

BaseTrainer.compute_loss implements exactly this step given a sampler and a buffer; other objectives override it.

docs.title: Generation (all objectives)
docs.text: A sampler drives the trained model through an integrator. MCMC samplers consume a score: an energy model is differentiated on the fly, a prediction_type="score" model passes through, an ("energy", "score") pair is indexed. FlowSampler integrates a velocity, score or noise prediction as an ODE or SDE on a uniform or custom time grid. Each piece can be swapped (e.g. integrator="heun" for "rk4") without changing the others.

docs.title: Time conditioning
docs.text:
Not all objectives condition the model on \( t \):

  • EquilibriumMatching: time-invariant; the model is called as model(x_t) in training and declares no prediction_type, so every sampler consumes the raw field: FlowSampler integrates it as the velocity and the gradient samplers apply \( x \leftarrow x + \eta f(x) \) to it.
  • FlowSampler with velocity/score models: time-conditional; the field is \( v(x, t) \) and the sampler feeds \( t \) every step.
  • EnergyMatching: the potential \(V(x)\) is time-independent; time lives in the temperature schedule of the generation sweep.

See examples/20-training for the reference loops.

docs.title: Code Guidelines
docs.text: Short version: simple, vectorised, consistent with PyTorch. Full rules below.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• PEP 8 enforced by black (line length 88) and isort (profile black).
  • Run both before every commit: 
    black torchebm/ tests/
isort torchebm/ tests/
  • Type hints on every public signature.
  • Google-style docstrings with raw strings (r"""..."""). LaTeX with \( \) inline and \[ \] for blocks. No Sphinx directives (:meth:, :attr:).
def sample_chain(
    dim: int,
    n_steps: int,
    n_samples: int = 1,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, dict]:
    r"""Run a Markov chain.

    Args:
        dim: Sample dimensionality.
        n_steps: Number of MCMC steps.
        n_samples: Number of parallel chains.

    Returns:
        Final samples and a diagnostics dict.
    """

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• Classes: CamelCase (LangevinDynamics)
  • Functions / variables: snake_case (compute_energy)
  • Constants: UPPER_CASE (DEFAULT_STEP_SIZE)

docs.title: API design
docs.text:
• Inherit from the matching base class (BaseLoss, BaseSampler, BaseModel, BaseIntegrator, BaseInterpolant). Do not invent parallel hierarchies.
  • Argument order is part of the API. Keep it consistent across samplers, losses, and integrators. When in doubt, match the closest existing component.
  • Explicit configuration: options are passed as constructor or call arguments.
  • Shallow inheritance. Compose objects; two levels of inheritance is usually the limit.

docs.title: Performance rules
docs.text:
These rules apply to all code in torchebm/:

  • Vectorise. No Python loops over batch elements.
  • No .item(), .cpu(), or .tolist() inside a hot loop.
  • Use self.device / self.dtype from TorchEBMModule. Never hard-code "cuda".
  • Inputs moved to device in BaseLoss.__call__. subclass forward() must not re-do it.
  • Wrap grad-free regions with torch.no_grad().
  • Use self.autocast_context() for mixed precision; it honours the module's configured dtype.

See Performance and Benchmarking for patterns and for when to measure.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• pytest for everything. Tests live under tests/ and mirror the torchebm/ layout.
  • File names: test_<module>.py. Function names: test_<behaviour>.
  • Use @pytest.fixture for shared setup and @pytest.mark.parametrize for table-driven tests (device, dtype, scale).
  • For stochastic code, seed once at the top of the test; mock torch.randn_like / torch.rand when you need exact equality.
  • Verify both correctness (finite output, shape, known analytical answer) and gradient flow (trainable params receive non-zero grads).

Run all tests, one package, or the suite with coverage:

pytest tests/ -v
pytest tests/losses -v
pytest --cov=torchebm

Benchmark and profile tests live under benchmarks/ and are disabled by default. see Performance and Benchmarking.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Every example folder under examples/ is smoke-tested in CI (pytest -m examples tests/examples, with TORCHEBM_SMOKE=1 shrinking iteration counts). When adding or touching an example, follow the conventions in examples/index.md and run the smoke suite before the PR.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not add docstrings, comments, or type hints to code you did not change.
  • Do not create one-shot helper modules. inline the operation.
  • Do not write markdown files (README, tutorial, guide) unless explicitly asked.
  • Do not edit files with shell redirection (cat >, echo >>, heredocs). Use the editor / file tools.
  • Do not introduce flake8 / pylint configs; black + isort + mypy are the configured tools.

docs.title: Distributed Training
docs.text:
TorchEBM leaves parallelism to the standard PyTorch wrappers: components never require an initialized process group, and no default forward() path of a model, loss or sampler issues a collective. You wrap the energy network, use your own launcher and data sharding, and the components behave identically. Collectives exist only behind explicit opt-ins (process_group= arguments and explicit methods) where the math is batch-global.

FSDP2 (fully_shard with DTensor parameters) is the primary target and the path validated on multi-GPU NCCL hardware. DDP also runs, but drives no design decisions.

docs.title: The shard-inside pattern
docs.text:
Shard the network inside your BaseModel subclass and keep the model object as the user-facing type. Samplers and losses stay unaware of sharding; every first-order path (energy calls, Langevin and HMC chains, CD, implicit EqM) runs through FSDP2's hooks unchanged.

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.distributed.fsdp import fully_shard
from torchebm.core import BaseModel

class EnergyMLP(BaseModel):
    def __init__(self, dim, hidden, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(dim, hidden), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, 1)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x).squeeze(-1)

model = EnergyMLP(dim=512, hidden=8192).cuda()
for m in model.net:
    if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
        fully_shard(m)
fully_shard(model.net)

The root call turns the parameters into sharded DTensors. Never wrap samplers or losses: losses see only model outputs and samplers call the model you pass them. TorchEBMModule resolves model.device and model.dtype correctly from DTensor parameters.

docs.title: Training loop (torchrun)
docs.text:
Persistent CD on a DistributedSampler-sharded loader, launched with torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 train.py; the model is built shard-inside as above:

import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torchebm.losses import ContrastiveDivergenceLoss
from torchebm.samplers import LangevinDynamics
from torchebm.utils import ReplayBuffer

rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
torch.cuda.set_device(int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]))
dist.init_process_group("nccl")
device = torch.device("cuda", torch.cuda.current_device())

model = build_sharded_energy()
sampler = LangevinDynamics(step_size=0.01)
loss_fn = ContrastiveDivergenceLoss()
buffer = ReplayBuffer(capacity=8192, sample_shape=(512,), device=device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)
generator = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(base_seed + rank)

for x in loader:
    x = x.to(device)
    x0 = buffer.sample(len(x), generator=generator)
    negatives = sampler(model, x0, n_steps=10, generator=generator)
    buffer.add(negatives)
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), model(negatives))
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

Three library-specific points, everything else is a standard FSDP2 loop:

  1. Pass a per-rank generator. The library holds no hidden RNG state; with a shared seed every rank draws identical start points and runs identical chains, and you pay for \(N\) GPUs to get one GPU of sample diversity. Generators are device-bound: create them on the compute device.
  2. Reduction semantics. Losses reduce with means over the local batch; with gradient averaging this equals the global-batch mean exactly when per-rank batch sizes are equal (keep drop_last=True).

  3. k-step MCMC and resharding. With default reshard-after-forward, every Langevin step re-gathers the parameters. For sampling-only loops (not inside a training forward/backward), hold them gathered:

    from torchebm.utils.distributed import unsharded

with unsharded(model.net):
    samples = sampler(model, x0, n_steps=500, generator=generator)

docs.title: Training through the score
docs.text:
FSDP2 hooks cannot run the double backward that training through the score needs (score matching, explicit EqM energies, energy matching): the post-backward hook reshards parameter storage that the second-order graph still references, independent of reshard_after_forward. A prediction_type="score" or ("energy", "score") model with DTensor parameters therefore takes a hook-free functional path, selected by giving it a template at construction:

from torchebm.losses import DenoisingScoreMatchingLoss

with torch.device("meta"):
    template = EnergyMLP(dim, hidden)
model = EnergyMLP(dim, hidden, prediction_type="score", functional_model=template)
shard(model)

loss_fn = DenoisingScoreMatchingLoss()
noise = torch.randn(x.shape, device=device, generator=generator)
loss = loss_fn(model(x + 0.1 * noise), -noise / 0.1)

The template supplies the module structure for torch.func.functional_call and its own parameters are never used, so it lives on the meta device. The sharded DTensor parameters are injected per call and the double backward runs through DTensor's differentiable collectives. Gradients match an unsharded reference with global-batch-mean semantics and land with the parameter's own placement (the per-rank contributions are reduce-scattered at accumulation time), so standard optimizers step them directly. Without a template, a score call under grad mode fails fast with an actionable error when it sees DTensor parameters. Energy matching and EqM-E train through the same call, so they shard the same way.

One dtype caveat: a bf16 MixedPrecisionPolicy affects the hook path only. The functional path reads the fp32 sharded parameters directly, so its compute stays fp32 regardless of the policy.

Under DDP the hook path handles the double backward; build the energy head without an output bias (the score does not depend on it) so every parameter receives a gradient with the default static_graph=False.

docs.title: PCD replay buffers across ranks
docs.text:
Persistent CD buffers are rank-local by design: each rank's ReplayBuffer keeps independent chains, so the world size multiplies chain diversity at zero cost, and no collective touches the buffer in the training step. To occasionally exchange chains between ranks, call the explicit collective between steps, on all ranks together:

buffer.mix_across_ranks()

It gathers the pooled chains, applies one shared permutation (drawn on rank 0 and broadcast, so per-rank generators cannot desynchronize it), and keeps the local shard: no chain is duplicated or lost.

docs.title: Global-batch OT coupling
docs.text:
Minibatch OT couplings are biased toward the batch size. With a process group, SinkhornCoupling solves on the pooled global batch instead, shrinking that bias at fixed per-rank batch size:

import torch.distributed as dist
from torchebm.couplings import SinkhornCoupling

coupling = SinkhornCoupling(reg=0.05, process_group=dist.group.WORLD)
x0, x1 = coupling(x0_local, x1_local, generator=generator)

Every rank gathers both batches, solves the identical pooled problem, and keeps its own targets, paired with sources from any rank; the per-target draw is broadcast from rank 0. Budget for the \((\text{world\_size} \times \text{batch})^2\) cost matrix on every rank. Exact and greedy couplings reject a process group (assignment solvers scale quadratically with the pooled batch); couple becomes a collective all ranks must enter together.

docs.title: EMA
docs.text:
update_ema works on sharded parameters when the EMA model and the training model are sharded identically (same mesh, same policy); each local shard updates in place with no collective. Copy before sharding, then shard both the same way:

ema = copy.deepcopy(model)
shard(model); shard(ema)
update_ema(ema, model, decay=0.999)

docs.title: Checkpointing
docs.text:
Sharded state takes the distributed checkpoint (one collective save); the replay buffer is rank-local state (PCD chains differ per rank) and goes to one plain file per rank:

import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import (
    get_model_state_dict, set_model_state_dict,
)

dcp.save({"model": get_model_state_dict(model)}, checkpoint_id=ckpt_dir)
torch.save(buffer.state_dict(), f"{ckpt_dir}/buffer_rank{rank}.pt")

state = {"model": get_model_state_dict(model)}
dcp.load(state, checkpoint_id=ckpt_dir)
set_model_state_dict(model, state["model"])
buffer.load_state_dict(torch.load(f"{ckpt_dir}/buffer_rank{rank}.pt"))

Do not put rank-local buffers into the DCP state dict: its planner deduplicates non-sharded tensors as replicated and silently keeps rank 0's chains. Restore rank-local files with the same world size, or re-initialize the buffer from noise (chains re-warm within a few hundred steps).

docs.title: Large-scale recipe
docs.text:
For models too large to materialize on one device, compose the standard FSDP2 ingredients; every piece is validated with TorchEBM components:

with torch.device("meta"):
    model = EnergyMLP(dim, hidden)
policy = MixedPrecisionPolicy(param_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
for m in model.net:
    if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
        fully_shard(m, mp_policy=policy)
fully_shard(model.net, mp_policy=policy)
model.to_empty(device="cuda")
torch.manual_seed(seed)
for m in model.net:
    if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
        m.reset_parameters()

The meta-device construction allocates no memory, to_empty materializes the local shards only, and the shared seed gives the same initialization on every rank. With a bf16 policy the score follows the input's dtype; set model.force_fp32_gradient = True if a low-precision model needs fp32-precision sampler gradients. Combine with the DCP checkpointing above.

docs.title: Other frameworks
docs.text:
The shard-inside pattern is framework-agnostic: anything that wraps an nn.Module composes the same way.

  • DDP: model.net = DistributedDataParallel(model.net). Everything runs, including training through the score, through the hooks.
  • DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 / HF Accelerate / Lightning Fabric: wrap or prepare the inner network, keep the BaseModel facade outside. The FSDP2 caveat carries over wherever parameters are partitioned: training through the score needs the functional path, which supports DTensor only, or a replica-style engine (ZeRO-½, DDP).
  • Tensor parallel (DTensor): the functional score path requires a 1-D device mesh; TP meshes are untested territory.

docs.title: Validation status
docs.text: The distributed test suite (pytest tests/distributed) runs 2-process gloo/CPU in CI and validates the contract; the same suite runs under NCCL with one process per GPU via TORCHEBM_DIST_DEVICE=cuda, and benchmarks/distributed_fsdp2.py exercises full CD and functional-DSM training steps at hundred-million-parameter scale on multi-GPU hardware.

docs.title: Performance and Benchmarking
docs.text: Patterns for writing performance-sensitive code, and the two measurement tools that back any performance claim: the benchmark suite (how fast is it?) and the profiler (where does the time go?).

docs.title: The four hot spots
docs.text:
1. Sampler steps: iterative, run 100-1000x, dominate wall time.
  2. Score / energy gradients: autograd.grad calls are frequent and stack.
  3. Loss forward + backward: called every training batch.
  4. Host-device traffic: .item(), .cpu(), repeated .to() stall the GPU.

Optimise in that order.

docs.title: Vectorise
docs.text:
Work in batch dimensions. A Python loop over samples launches one kernel per sample:

energies = torch.stack([energy_fn(x[i]) for i in range(batch)])

The batched call computes all (batch,) energies in one pass:

energies = energy_fn(x)

Sample many chains in parallel by putting the chain index in the leading dim.

docs.title: Stay on device
docs.text:
Keep tensors on one device and dtype for the whole pipeline. Use self.device / self.dtype from TorchEBMModule inside the library; never hard-code "cuda".

.item(), .cpu(), .tolist(), and Python if tensor > 0: all trigger a full GPU sync. This loop stalls the GPU at every step:

for step in range(n_steps):
    loss = loss_fn(x)
    if loss.item() < threshold:
        break

Keeping the values on device and reading them once after the loop costs a single sync:

losses = []
for step in range(n_steps):
    losses.append(loss_fn(x).detach())
avg = torch.stack(losses).mean().item()

docs.title: The GPU-first contract
docs.text:
Every new sampler, loss, or trainer honours these rules; the existing components already do:

  • Normalise transfers once at entry, never per step. Move conditioning and inputs to the device a single time when a call begins, then reuse them. TorchEBMModule._prepare_model_kwargs is the reference: it device-aligns model_kwargs once and the per-step drift closures capture the result.
  • No .item() / .cpu() / .tolist() / .numpy() inside a step loop. Diagnostics and metrics stay device tensors and are stacked, then synced once at a logging boundary (BaseTrainer.train_step returns device scalars; train_epoch syncs once per epoch). Preallocate trajectories/diagnostics on device and fill them in place.
  • Host scalars enter only through schedulers. get_scheduled_value returns a Python float computed on the host, so it folds into the next kernel launch with no device→host sync. Do not read step sizes or temperatures back off a device tensor.
  • Respect the input dtype. The autograd score of a prediction_type="score" model computes in the input's dtype (byte-identical for float32, no fp64 downcast); set model.force_fp32_gradient = True only when a low-precision model needs an fp32-precision score.
  • Adaptive/implicit integrators carry one bounded sync per iteration (the step-acceptance and solver-convergence checks are data-dependent and must reach the host). This is inherent; fixed-step integrators are the sync-free path. Greedy OT coupling is likewise host-bound by nature - use Sinkhorn in the training loop.

To catch a regression, wrap a hot loop in torch.cuda.set_sync_debug_mode("error"): any accidental host sync raises with the offending op named.

docs.title: Reuse memory
docs.text:
Pre-allocate buffers once and fill them in place inside loops. The samplers write a trajectory into one pre-allocated tensor:

trajectory = x.new_empty((x.shape[0], n_steps, *x.shape[1:]))
for i in range(n_steps):
    x = integrator.step({"x": x}, step_size, drift=drift)["x"]
    trajectory[:, i] = x

In-place ops (x.add_, x.mul_) are safe outside autograd-tracked paths.

docs.title: Mixed precision and compilation
docs.text: Inside the library, wrap large matmul blocks with self.autocast_context(), which honours the user's configured dtype. At the benchmark/application layer, --amp and --compile apply the same transforms via benchmarks/registry.py::apply_mode, so eager, compiled, and mixed-precision results stay comparable.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Implicit host-device copies: torch.tensor(x_numpy, device=...) inside a loop.
  • Redundant .to() calls: BaseLoss.__call__ already moves inputs; subclass forward() must not.
  • Missing torch.no_grad(): interpolation targets, momentum init, and random projections need no grad tracking.
  • Tiny batches on GPU: prefer one big step over many small ones.
  • isinstance checks inside the inner loop: resolve once before the loop.

docs.title: Benchmarks: detecting change
docs.text:
The suite (pytest-benchmark under benchmarks/) auto-discovers every component exported from torchebm.*.__init__ and times its standard workload at three scales. Regular pytest tests/ never runs them.

Command Runs bash benchmarks/run.sh --quick a smoke run at small scale bash benchmarks/run.sh --module losses one module bash benchmarks/run.sh --filter "ScoreMatching" the benchmarks matching a name bash benchmarks/run.sh --baseline the suite, saving the results as the baseline bash benchmarks/run.sh --compare a comparison of the latest two runs bash benchmarks/run.sh --ci the suite, failing if the geo-mean speedup is below 0.95x

Components needing non-default construction get an entry in benchmarks/registry.py::COMPONENT_OVERRIDES; existing entries are the best reference. Modules and individual benchmarks can be excluded in benchmarks/benchmark.toml.

Publishing. Results and the dashboard live in the separate torchebm-benchmarks repository, deployed at soran-ghaderi.github.io/torchebm-benchmarks. After a run: copy the autosaved JSON from benchmarks/results/Linux-CPython-*/ into that repo and run bash scripts/publish.sh <path-to-json>; GitHub Pages auto-deploys.

docs.title: Profiling: explaining change
docs.text:
benchmarks/profiler.py wraps torch.profiler around the same registry callables the benchmarks time. Profile only when an optimisation is non-trivial and evidence-driven: a dashboard regression to localise, a hot path rewrite to justify, or a suspected memory issue. Skip it for one-line fixes and cleanups.

The workflow is one profile before the change, one after it, and a diff:

python benchmarks/profiler.py run --component LangevinDynamics --scale medium --top 20 --label before
python benchmarks/profiler.py run --component LangevinDynamics --scale medium --top 20 --label after
python benchmarks/profiler.py diff benchmarks/profiles/*_before benchmarks/profiles/*_after

Add --trace only when the top-N table is not enough (open in ui.perfetto.dev), --memory for allocator work (view at pytorch.org/memory_viz), --nvtx for Nsight Systems. Arbitrary callables profile via --callable module:factory. Outputs land under benchmarks/profiles/ (gitignored; profiles are local by design).

Division of labour: benchmarks detect a regression and track it across releases; the profiler explains it op by op on one run.

docs.title: What is TorchEBM, and what is it not?
docs.text: TorchEBM is a PyTorch library of composable primitives for generative models that learn dynamics on data space: energies and fields, samplers, losses, interpolants, couplings, integrators, and schedulers. It covers EBMs, diffusion, flow matching, and equilibrium and energy matching; Schrödinger bridges, flow maps, and discrete or manifold state spaces are on the roadmap. It ships no pretrained checkpoints and no dataset loaders beyond the 2D synthetic benchmarks, and BaseTrainer is a thin wrapper around the training loop. See Design and Scope.

docs.title: Is every model in TorchEBM an energy-based model?
docs.text: No. Energy-based models are the case where the model is a scalar potential and samples come from its gradient. Flow-matching velocities, diffusion scores and the implicit equilibrium-matching field are vector fields that need not be gradients of any energy. The library takes its name from EBMs; the Design and Scope page places both kinds of model.

docs.title: How does it relate to diffusers, torchdiffeq, or POT?
docs.text: diffusers ships production diffusion pipelines around pretrained checkpoints; TorchEBM ships the mathematical components those methods are made of, for research on the methods themselves. torchdiffeq provides general ODE solvers; TorchEBM implements its own integrator layer (fixed-step, adaptive, implicit, symplectic) shared by MCMC and flow sampling, with no external solver dependency. POT is a general OT toolbox; TorchEBM likewise implements its own coupling layer, the pairing rules its transport-based objectives consume, shared across the library with no external OT dependency.

docs.title: Which training objective should I use?
docs.text: The decision table in Learning Objectives is the full answer. In brief: contrastive divergence when you need a calibrated energy and can afford MCMC inside the loss; denoising score matching for sampling-free EBM training; equilibrium matching for generative quality with few integration steps; energy matching when one time-independent potential should serve both transport and Boltzmann sampling.

docs.title: How do samplers and integrators compose?
docs.text: Every sampler accepts integrator= as a registry name or instance: LangevinDynamics and HMC use it for their dynamics, FlowSampler for ODE/SDE generation. get_integrator("rk4") constructs one directly. The integrator comparison example measures the accuracy orders.

docs.title: Why do I see deprecation warnings about model-bound losses and samplers?
docs.text:
TorchEBM moved to the standard PyTorch loop: losses consume model outputs and samplers take the model at call time. The old forms keep working and warn once per process.

Deprecated Use instead ContrastiveDivergence(model, sampler), PersistentContrastiveDivergence ContrastiveDivergenceLoss()(model(x), model(x_neg)) with x_neg = sampler(model, x0, n_steps=k); a ReplayBuffer holds persistent chains FlowMatchingLoss(model=...), EquilibriumMatchingLoss(model=...), EnergyMatchingLoss(model=...) the same classes without model: x_t, u_t = path(x0, x1, t) then loss_fn(model(x_t, t), u_t) ScoreMatching, DenoisingScoreMatching, SlicedScoreMatching ScoreMatchingLoss, DenoisingScoreMatchingLoss, SlicedScoreMatchingLoss on the output of a prediction_type="score" model LangevinDynamics(model=...), HamiltonianMonteCarlo(model=...), FlowSampler(model=...) and sampler.sample(x=...) sampler(model, x, n_steps=...) FlowSampler(prediction=, negate_velocity=, train_eps=) prediction_type= on the model or the sampler; trained fields point from noise to data EqMEnergy a prediction_type="score" model sampled directly model.gradient(x) model(x) on a model built with prediction_type="score", which returns \(-\nabla_x E\); a closed-form gradient goes in AnalyticModel._score ContrastiveDivergenceTrainer BaseTrainer(model, optimizer, ContrastiveDivergenceLoss(), sampler=..., buffer=...) ReflowCoupling(flow) x1 = sampler(model, x0, n_steps=...) in the training loop EMA(model, decay=d) torch.optim.swa_utils.AveragedModel(model, multi_avg_fn=get_ema_multi_avg_fn(d)) with ema.update_parameters(model); sample from ema.module.eval()

The deprecated paths are removed in release 0.12.0, and not before 2027-01-29; tests/test_deprecations.py enforces the window. The scripts in examples/20-training show each loop in full.

docs.title: How do I define a custom energy?
docs.text: Subclass BaseModel with any differentiable forward mapping (N, d) to (N,); built with prediction_type="score" or ("energy", "score"), the call returns the autograd score. See The Energy-Based View and the custom energies example.

docs.title: Do I need a GPU?
docs.text: No. Every example and test runs on CPU; the library is device-agnostic and components accept a device= argument. A GPU matters for training neural energies and for large chain counts, where vectorized sampling scales linearly.

docs.title: Why do my Langevin samples diverge or collapse?
docs.text: The usual causes are a step size too large for the energy's curvature (diverges) or a noise scale of zero (collapses to a mode; that is gradient descent). Anneal with a scheduler, as in the scheduler anatomy example, and prefer smooth activations (SiLU, GELU) in neural energies so the force field stays well behaved.

docs.title: How are the examples kept correct?
docs.text: Every example folder is executed by CI as a smoke test (pytest -m examples tests/examples) with TORCHEBM_SMOKE=1 shrinking iteration counts. If an API change breaks an example, the build fails.

docs.title: Where do benchmarks live?
docs.text: On the external dashboard at soran-ghaderi.github.io/torchebm-benchmarks, generated from benchmarks/ runs in this repository. The performance guide describes the workflow.

docs.title: Are Schrödinger bridges supported?
docs.text: Not yet. Bridge matching needs a probability path with a latent term \(\gamma(t) z\), which the interpolants do not have yet, and an SDE sampler that consumes a learned velocity and score together; iterative proportional fitting also needs simulation inside the training loop. The couplings (including entropic OT) and the SDE integrators already exist, and the design page lists the gap.

docs.title: How do I cite TorchEBM?
docs.text: Use the BibTeX entry on the home page. GitHub also serves it from CITATION.cff through the "Cite this repository" button, which exports BibTeX and APA.

docs.title: How do I contribute?
docs.text:
Start with the Developer Guide: environment setup, code guidelines, and the PR workflow. Adding an example is a good first contribution; the recipe is in the examples overview.

Questions not covered here: open an issue.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: TorchEBM provides composable PyTorch primitives for generative models that learn dynamics on data space, from energy-based models to diffusion, flow matching, and equilibrium and energy matching: energies and fields, samplers, losses, interpolants, couplings, integrators, and schedulers. This page takes you from installation to the core workflows the library is built around.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install torchebm

The only hard dependencies are PyTorch and NumPy. A CUDA-enabled PyTorch build is recommended for training; every snippet below also runs on CPU.

docs.title: Sample from an energy
docs.text:
An energy \(E(x)\) defines a density \(p(x) \propto e^{-E(x)}\). Samplers draw from it using only the energy's gradient, here with Langevin dynamics. The model is an argument of the call, as the function is for torchdiffeq:

import torch
from torchebm.core import GaussianModel
from torchebm.samplers import LangevinDynamics

model = GaussianModel(mean=torch.zeros(2), cov=torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.8], [0.8, 1.0]]))
sampler = LangevinDynamics(step_size=0.02, noise_scale=1.0)

samples = sampler(model, torch.randn(2000, 2), n_steps=500)
print(torch.cov(samples.T))

Every sampler is vectorized over chains: the call above runs 2000 independent chains as one tensor program and recovers the target covariance. Swap in HamiltonianMonteCarlo or change integrator= without touching the rest.

docs.title: Train an energy from data
docs.text:
Any differentiable module mapping (N, d) to (N,) is a valid energy. Train it with contrastive divergence: the sampler draws negatives from the current model and the loss compares the energies of data and negatives:

import torch
from torch import nn
from torchebm.core import BaseModel
from torchebm.datasets import TwoMoonsDataset
from torchebm.losses import ContrastiveDivergenceLoss
from torchebm.samplers import LangevinDynamics

class MLP(BaseModel):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(128, 1),
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x).squeeze(-1)

data = TwoMoonsDataset(n_samples=3000, noise=0.05, seed=0).get_data()
model = MLP()
sampler = LangevinDynamics(step_size=0.1, noise_scale=1.0)
loss_fn = ContrastiveDivergenceLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for step in range(1000):
    batch = data[torch.randint(len(data), (256,))]
    negatives = sampler(model, batch, n_steps=10)
    loss = loss_fn(model(batch), model(negatives))
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

docs.title: Train a generative flow
docs.text:
The same library expresses continuous-time generation. Equilibrium matching regresses a time-invariant field onto the velocity of the interpolant path, and FlowSampler integrates it from noise:

import torch
from torch import nn
from torchebm.datasets import TwoMoonsDataset
from torchebm.interpolants import LinearInterpolant
from torchebm.losses import EquilibriumMatchingLoss
from torchebm.samplers import FlowSampler

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 256), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Linear(256, 2),
        )
    def forward(self, x, t=None, **kwargs):
        return self.net(x)

data = TwoMoonsDataset(n_samples=4000, noise=0.05, seed=0).get_data()
model = MLP()
path = LinearInterpolant()
loss_fn = EquilibriumMatchingLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for step in range(3000):
    x1 = data[torch.randint(len(data), (256,))]
    x0 = torch.randn_like(x1)
    t = torch.rand(len(x1))
    x_t, u_t = path(x0, x1, t)
    loss = loss_fn(model(x_t), u_t, t)
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

sampler = FlowSampler(integrator="euler")
samples = sampler(model, torch.randn(4000, 2), n_steps=100)

Each piece is chosen independently: the interpolant selects the probability path, the integrator string selects the numerics, and a coupling called before the interpolant selects how noise is paired with data.
